title: Even with those you dislike
hookLine: don't let hatred of a people make you unjust, be just (5:8)
last: THE WUDU VERSE — THE WASHING, WRITTEN.

lines: THE NAME THAT MAKES YOUR SHOULDERS RISE.
cards: Scroll through your contacts and one name may make your shoulders rise. A coworker. An ex.
The cousin who ruins every holiday. Now someone asks you to describe your last argument with them, and asks for one thing only: be accurate. Not kind.
Accurate. Fair to the person you can't stand is a different muscle. Fair to a whole group you resent is harder still.

Surah five was given to a community that had real opponents, people who had fought them and turned them away from Mecca. Twice in this one surah, the Qur'an stops to say the same hard thing about them.

teach.b: First, verse two, three days back: don't let hatred of the people who barred you from the Sacred Mosque push you into wrongdoing. The second is verse eight, today's.
In Pickthall's words: “let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.”
The Arabic word for that hatred is shana'an, a deep, settled dislike, the kind that has history.
The verse opens by telling believers to be qawwamin, people who stand up and keep standing, as witnesses for Allah in fairness.

Set it beside 4:135, from a week ago: stand for justice even against yourselves, your parents, your kin. Commentators pair the two verses. One guards against bending the truth for the people you love.
The other guards against bending it against the people you hate.

teach.h: LOVE AND HATE BOTH TIP THE SCALES.
teach.b: Love and hate pull the scales in opposite directions, and the Qur'an names both. A hadith report tells of a companion, Abdullah ibn Rawaha, sent to assess a harvest at Khaybar for people who had been at war with Medina.

He told them, more or less: I come from the person I love most, and you are not dear to me, but neither will make me unfair to you. They are said to have answered that this is what holds up the heavens and the earth.
And notice the reason the verse gives. Not that your enemy deserves it.
That justice is nearer to taqwa, to living aware of God.
The fairness is about who you are, not about who they are.

how: Muslim jurists and teachers cite 5:8 as the ground of fair dealing with opponents, in courts, in trade and in war, and it is often recalled when anger at a whole group of people runs high.

o: a sudden flash of anger that passes
a deep, settled hatred with a history
a feud passed down between two tribes

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: those who stand up and keep standing
justice even against yourself and kin
justice even toward those you dislike

s: the warning about hatred appears twice in surah five
in verse two and again in verse eight.
the verse says be fair because your enemy deserves it
it says justice is nearer to taqwa: the reason is about the one being fair.
commentators read 4:135 and 5:8 as a pair
one guards against bias for those you love, the other against bias against those you dislike.

games.q: you're Abdullah ibn Rawaha, sent to assess the harvest of people who fought your city. what do you do?
o: estimate fairly, and tell them why.
games.why: the report says he told them neither his love for the Prophet nor his feelings about them would make him unfair, and they said this is what holds up the heavens and the earth.

practice: Bring that person to mind and try to say one true thing in their favor: not a compliment you don't mean, just something accurate, like they work hard, or they were right about that one thing.
If nothing comes, stay with the breath and let the question sit.

wordCard.voice: Shana'an. The old, settled hatred the Qur'an says must never bend you from being fair, even to the people you resent.

orig.note: Arabic: justice, fairness, setting things level. 5:8 uses the verb: i'dilu, deal justly.

carryVoice: Your line: just, even then. Love and hate both tip the scales. And that's another week.

sources.q: let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.

sources.ref: the report of Abdullah ibn Rawaha at Khaybar (Muwatta Malik; Musnad Ahmad)
